notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Genesis 36:1–22 below, but there are three gaps you should know about first:

- **I found no real disagreement between Protestant traditions.** The commentators I read come from different traditions: Gill (Baptist and Calvinist), Clarke (Wesleyan), Coffman (Restoration Movement), the Geneva Study Bible (Reformed), Kretzmann (Lutheran) and Guzik at enduringword. None of them argues against another tradition on these verses. The differences I did find are between individual commentators, mainly over how kindly to judge Esau.
- **I couldn't reach several of the sites you listed.** I ran out of searches before getting to netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic and Orthodox sites, or anything on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. The Catholic material I saw was only the Douay-Rheims translation, with no commentary.
- **Verses 13 and 18–19 have little or nothing,** and I haven't filled the gaps myself.

---

**v. 1 – "the account of Esau (that is, Edom)"**
- Guzik says the Edomites are descended from Esau, Isaac's son and Jacob's twin.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/
- Bible Hub's study note says "This is the account" marks a new section of Genesis, like the earlier "accounts" (2:4; 5:1; 25:12, 19; 37:2).  It adds that the name "Edom" ("red") recalls the red stew Esau traded his birthright for.  https://biblehub.com/genesis/36-1.htm
- Benson gives reasons the line is recorded at all: Esau's link to Abraham and Isaac; Edom being Israel's neighbour; and fulfilment of the promise that Abraham would father many nations, of "two nations are in thy womb", and of Isaac's blessing on Esau.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-1.htm
- Gill quotes the Jewish scholar Maimonides: the rest of Esau's line had to be recorded carefully because Amalek, one branch of it, was to be destroyed by God's command. Otherwise the whole family might have perished together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-1.htm
- Matthew Henry says the name Edom keeps alive the memory of the foolish trade. He thinks this explains why Esau's family gets such a short account.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_036.cfm
- The Geneva Study Bible (Reformed) says the genealogy shows Esau was blessed in worldly things.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-1.htm
- **Scholarly debate:** The Cambridge Bible calls "the same is Edom" a gloss, a note added later, here and in vv. 8 and 19. Barnes disagrees: he sees these clauses as signs of an early, simple style, not clear evidence of later revision. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-1.htm

**v. 2 – Adah and Oholibamah**
- Guzik says this marriage went against the family's values. Abraham had been determined that Isaac would not marry a Canaanite.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/
- **The names problem:** The wives' names differ from those in 26:34 and 28:9. Clarke thinks the women simply had other names: Aholibamah is Judith, Adah is Bashemath, and this chapter's Basemath is Mahalath.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-2.html
- Ellicott has a different solution: Judith had no children, Adah is listed first because she was the first wife to bear sons, and Aholibamah was a fourth and last wife.  https://biblehub.com/genesis/36-2.htm
- The bible.org study guide gives both options (four wives, or wives with more than one name). It also notes the Hebrew text says "daughter of Zibeon" while the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint and Syriac read "son". From context and v. 24 it concludes a granddaughter is meant. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-36
- The Bible Hub study note reads Oholibamah's name, "tent of the high place", as a hint of the religious mixing that would mark Edom.  https://biblehub.com/genesis/36-2.htm

**v. 3 – Basemath, daughter of Ishmael**
- Bible.org: she is called Mahalath in 28:9, and Esau married her to please his parents. Nebaioth may be named because Ishmael had died and her brother gave her in marriage. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-36

**vv. 4–5 – Esau's sons born in Canaan**
- Matthew Henry notes three wives produced only five sons. He comments that God often frustrates people who build a family by improper means, yet here the promise won out.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_036.cfm
- Bible.org on Korah: some see two different Korahs (v. 5 and v. 16). The medieval rabbi Rashi linked them through a story of incest. The writer calls that typical of Jewish bias against Esau and says the text doesn't spell it out. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-36

**v. 6 – Esau moves away**
- The Geneva Study Bible sees God's providence here: the wicked make way for the godly, so Jacob can have Canaan as promised.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-6.htm
- Poole gives three reasons for the move. Esau chose hunting country, his wives pressed him, and above all Providence was quietly at work.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-6.htm
- **Does this contradict 32:3, where Esau already lives in Seir?** Keil and Delitzsch say no: Esau settled in Seir knowing Jacob, as heir, would take over the family land.  Benson thinks Esau kept some property in Canaan while Isaac lived and withdrew completely after Isaac died. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-6.htm
- **Text note:** The Cambridge Bible says the Syriac reads "the land of Seir" and this may be the original wording.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-6.htm

**v. 7 – Too much wealth to live together**
- Guzik says Esau's earlier cry, "Have you only one blessing, my father?" (27:38), turned out to be unfounded.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/
- Ellicott compares it to Abraham and Lot parting. He suggests Esau may have chosen Seir because, through Aholibamah, he was a chief there.  https://biblehub.com/genesis/36-7.htm
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) sees here how great wealth divides people.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-7.html

**v. 8 – Esau settles in Mount Seir**
- Guzik: this land lay south and east of the Dead Sea and came to be called Edom.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/
- Matthew Henry says God gave Seir to Esau (Deut 2:5; Josh 24:4). He adds that Esau, who had fought for Canaan, now quietly withdraws. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_036.cfm

**v. 9 – "father of the Edomites"**
- Guzik notes Edom is mentioned about 130 times in Scripture. Edom refused Israel passage in the wilderness (Num 20:21), yet God told Israel not to despise an Edomite as a brother (Deut 23:7).  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/
- Barnes: the repeated heading separates Esau's family history in Seir from his history in Canaan.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-12.htm

**v. 10**
- Bible.org: the repeated lists of sons show the chapter is built from several separate genealogical records. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-36

**v. 11 – The sons of Eliphaz**
- Barnes links Teman to the Temanites, the people of Eliphaz the Temanite in Job.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-12.htm

**v. 12 – Timna and Amalek**
- Guzik: Amalek was the ancestor of the Amalekites, notable enemies of Israel.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/
- Bible.org's notes say Timna is singled out because she was the mother of Israel's fierce enemy. They read the mention as deliberately unflattering, since this is the only child of a concubine in the list.  https://bible.org/book/export/html/20859
- Clarke (Wesleyan): Timna was Lotan the Horite's sister (v. 22), which shows how Esau's family and the Horites intermarried. This may have given Esau's sons an excuse to seize the land (Deut 2:12).  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-12.html
- Gill (Baptist) records a rabbinic claim that Timna was both Eliphaz's daughter and his concubine. He notes Israel was later commanded to destroy the Amalekites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-12.htm
- **Where Amalek came from is debated.** One commentator on the Bible Hub page doubts so great a people could come from a concubine, given Balaam's phrase "first among the nations" (Num 24:20).  Another argues the Amalekites who attacked Israel did descend from this Amalek, and rejects the Arab legend of an older Amalek.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-12.htm

**v. 14**
- Barnes: Oholibamah's sons are younger than the other wives' sons, so they are listed separately.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-12.htm

**vv. 15–17 – The chiefs ("dukes")**
- JFB: the word means a tribal head, like a sheikh or a highland clan chief, not a British duke.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_036.cfm
- Barnes: the ten grandsons rank with Oholibamah's three sons, which suggests she was the last wife.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-2.html
- Guzik ties all these chiefs to "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated" (Mal 1:2–3; Rom 9:13). He reads it as Esau being blessed materially but not chosen to inherit the covenant.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/
- Matthew Henry warns against overvaluing titles:  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_036.cfm

**v. 20 – Seir the Horite**
- Ellicott: the Horite list is included partly for Oholibamah's family tree, but mainly because the Horites merged with Esau's descendants to form the Edomites.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-20.htm
- Benson sees it as a lasting rebuke to the Edomites for marrying into the Horites and picking up their ways.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-20.htm
- Clarke: the Horites were the original people of Seir, driven out by Esau's descendants.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-20.html
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) describes them as cave-dwellers who shared the caves with their flocks.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/genesis-36.html
- **Scholarly note:** Bible.org says "Horite" usually means the non-Semitic Hurrians, but these may have been Semitic miners or cave-dwellers, since all the names are Semitic.  https://bible.org/book/export/html/20859

**v. 21**
- Clarke, following the scholar Calmet, says the Horite chiefs and Esau's chiefs must have lived at the same time, mixed together in one land. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-21.html
- Gill: these chiefs lived there before the land was called Edom, and their descendants later paid tribute to Edom.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-21.html
- Guzik notes Dishon means "gazelle". He takes the names in this line as not reflecting a godly heart.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/

**v. 22 – Lotan and Timna**
- Barnes: Hori has the same name as the nation; Hemam is spelled Homam in Chronicles; and this Timna is Eliphaz's concubine from v. 12.  He thinks she was probably a very young sister of Lotan.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/36-12.html

---

**How harshly to judge Esau (cuts across traditions)**
- **Harsh readings:** Matthew Henry calls Esau a lasting despiser of heavenly things. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-1.htm The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says God's enemies can enjoy great worldly glory.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/genesis-36.html
- **Kinder readings:** The Pulpit Commentary credits Esau with leaving peacefully instead of fighting Jacob for the land.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html Coffman sees the chapter as being fair to Esau, who left of his own accord to avoid conflict.  https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/genesis-36.html
- **Jewish readings:** The bible.org writer warns that negative rabbinic readings of Esau come from bias that the text doesn't support. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-36
